purpose: Disulfiram is used to help people who are recovering from alcohol addiction stay sober. It is not a cure for alcoholism, but it acts as a strong deterrent to drinking. It works best when used as part of a full treatment program that includes counseling and support.
how_it_works: Normally, your body breaks down alcohol in two steps. Disulfiram blocks the second step, causing a toxic substance called acetaldehyde to build up in your blood if you drink alcohol. This buildup causes very unpleasant symptoms — like flushing, nausea, and a racing heart — that make drinking feel terrible, which discourages you from drinking.
common_side_effects: When taken without alcohol, side effects are usually mild and may include drowsiness, tiredness, headache, a metallic or garlic-like taste in your mouth, and mild skin rash. These often improve after the first couple of weeks.
warnings: NEVER drink alcohol while taking this medication — even small amounts found in mouthwash, cough syrups, cooking wines, or vinegar-based foods can trigger a severe reaction. Reactions can include chest pain, difficulty breathing, vomiting, very low blood pressure, and in rare cases can be life-threatening. Tell your doctor if you have heart disease, liver problems, diabetes, or a history of mental illness. Do not take your first dose until you have not had alcohol for at least 12 hours. This medication should never be given to a patient without their full knowledge and consent.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 500 mg once daily for 1 to 2 weeks, then reduced to a maintenance dose of 250 mg once daily. Your doctor will adjust your dose based on how you respond. It is typically taken in the morning, but if it makes you drowsy, your doctor may suggest taking it at bedtime.
